8. The appellate court though upheld the finding and decision of the trial court that the defendant No. 1 was not adopted son of Purna Chandra, but it set aside the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by limitation and that the defendant No. 1 being the domesticated son-in-law of the original owner Purna Chandra he cannot be evicted from the property of his lather-in-law. 

 9. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree of the appellate court the plaintiff filed the above mentioned civil revision and the revisional court set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court and restored those of the trial court making observations that the question of limitation being not raised specifically in pleadings and in deposition, the question of limitation cannot be decided in this suit and the appellate court's finding that the suit is barred by limitation, therefore, is not sustainable. The revisional court rejected the appellate court's further finding that a domesticated son-in-law is entitled to the right of residence, possession and maintenance from the estate of his father-in-law making no clear observation as to whether it accepted the appellate court's findings the defendant No. 1 is the domesticated son-in-law of Purna Chandra. 

 15. It appears that the main question for determination before the trial court was whether the defendant No. 1 was the adopted son of Purna Chandra. The trial court, on consideration of evidence-both oral and documentary adduced before it found that the defendant No. 1 was not the adopted son of Purna Chandra. The appellate court also, on consideration of all these evidence, concurred with the finding of the trial court that the defendant No. 1 was not the adopted son of Purna Chandra. But it appears that the appellate court dismissed the suit holding that it was barred by limitation though no such question of limitation was raised by either of the two contesting defendants in their pleadings or deposition. However, the revisional court, on consideration of evidence on record; rightly pointed out that in the pleadings of both the contesting defendant Nos.1 and 2 there was not a single word as to limitation and therefore, no issue was framed by the trial court regarding limitation and no evidence also was adduced as to limitation which is a mixed question of fact and law. The revisional court thus rightly observed also that unless the point of limitation is specifically raised in the written statement and unless there is evidence on this point by the D.Ws. the question of limitation cannot be raised and decided in the suit and as such the appellate court's finding that the suit is barred by limitation is not sustainable at all.
